endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Organizations should elevate this designation formally, specifying decision-making rights and reporting obligations.

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether periodic governance review of cumulative risk across multiple AI tools reduces cascading errors or staff burden, and no supplied study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation rests on a single framework endorsement, so health systems adopting it are acting on expert judgment rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated when no comparison exists, so this recommendation carries no direct evidence. The single supporting source is a framework document, which reflects consensus opinion and does not supply effect estimates.

The supplied material contains no study showing that interacting AI tools compound errors or add staff burden beyond what single-tool review detects. Without such data, the size and frequency of cascading harm remain unmeasured, and a governance body cannot yet judge which tool combinations deserve the most scrutiny or whether joint review catches errors that separate reviews miss.

One source, the CHAI governance playbooks, endorses the practice at a "should" level. The quoted language addresses formal designation of decision-making rights and reporting obligations, which describes governance structure rather than a specific method for assessing cumulative risk. No supplied regulation or statute is cited as requiring cross-tool risk evaluation.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that first measure how often errors or workload increases arise from interactions among AI tools sharing workflows, patients, or staff, and then compare organizations or periods with and without periodic cumulative-risk review on outcomes such as error propagation, alert burden, and patient harm. Such work would also need to define what a cumulative-risk review consists of so that it can be replicated.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It remains unknown whether cumulative AI risk falls more heavily on these groups, for example in safety-net settings where lean staffing may concentrate several tools on the same clinicians, and any future evaluation would need to sample these populations deliberately.
